From op + mars, calque of German Aufmarsch.

parole.significato: the act of absorbing or assimilating, uptake, absorption
parole.testo: Derived from opnemen on the model of German Aufnahme, which is deverbal (with ablaut) from aufnehmen; compare the etymology at Proto-Germanic *nēmō. The same is true of other nouns in -name.
From 16th century. Calque of German Aufenthalt.
From German optisch, analyzable as optiek + -isch.
From op + tocht. Perhaps a calque of German Aufzug.
From op (“up”) + wind (“wind, draft”), calque of German Aufwind.
Borrowed from German Ordner, from Briefordner. Equivalent to a shortening of briefordner.
Borrowed from German organisch.

parole.significato: orgastic (experiencing, resembling or pertaining to orgasm; having the character of an orgasm)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German orgastisch or French orgastique. Equivalent to orgasme + -isch with -t- replacing -m- as seen in some other Greek roots.
Borrowed from German Orthodontie or French orthodontie.
Calque of German übrigens, based on overig.
Calque of German Übernahme, deverbal from overnemen. The same is true of other nouns in -name.
Borrowed from German überreden.
Borrowed from German überrumpeln (16th century).

parole.significato: to outstrip, to overshadow, to eclipse
parole.testo: 19th century, from over- (“over”) + vleugel (“flank”, literally “wing”) + -en, a calque of German überflügeln (18th c.).

parole.significato: to import in excess, so that demand is over-saturated
parole.testo: The Woordenboek der Nederlandsche Taal considers this a calque of German überführen. The Deutsches Wörterbuch does indeed the attest the phrase den Markt überführen (“to oversaturate the market”). From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour.
From Pasen + haas, calque of German Osterhase.
Probably a borrowing from German Paläolithikum. First attested in the early 20th century.

parole.significato: a type of palace, a temporary imperial or royal residence for a sovereign without a fixed, centralised capital
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Pfalz, ultimately from Latin palātium. Doublet of paleis.
Probably borrowed from German Paludarium. Equivalent to Latin palūs, palūdis (“marsh, swamp”) + -arium.
Borrowed from German Pangermanismus. Equivalent to pan- + germaan + -isme.
Either borrowed from German Pangermanismus or formed from either pangermanistisch or pangermanisme.
Borrowed German panisch, from Middle French panice, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós).

parole.significato: the doctrine that all matter has a mental aspect; panpsychism
parole.testo: Formed by the prefixation of pan- + psychism after the German Panpsychismus (1874), itself after the Latin pampsychia (1591). Compare the Ancient Greek πάμψυχος (pámpsukhos, “in full life”) and the Modern Greek παμψυχισμός (pampsychismós, “panpsychism”).
Probably borrowed from German Panslawist, equivalent to pan- + Slaaf + -ist. First attested in 1847, but not common until the 1860s.
Borrowed from German panslawistisch. Equivalent to panslavist + -isch.

parole.significato: antihero, especially a henpecked one who merely talks the talk
parole.testo: 19th century. Borrowed from German Pantoffelheld, equivalent to pantoffel (“house slipper”) + held (“hero”).

parole.significato: sweet pepper, bell pepper (plant or fruit of Capsicum annuum varieties yielding sweet peppers)
parole.testo: From German Paprika, from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar (“pepper”), from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi), from an Indo-Aryan language.
Borrowed from German Pardel.
Borrowed from German Parlamentarier.

parole.significato: a political supporter, especially of a political party or faction
parole.testo: Compound of partij + ganger. The sense “political supporter” derives from German Parteigänger.
Borrowed from German patent, originating in student slang. Related to etymology 1.
From German Patrone, ultimately from Latin patrōnus.

parole.significato: kettledrum, usually in the plural: timpani
parole.testo: From German Pauke.

From German Pech (“bad luck; pitch, tar”), from Old High German peh, from Latin pīx. Doublet of inherited pek (“pitch”). Also cognate with English pitch. The sense “breakdown” is a Dutch innovation. It is probably modelled on the word ongeluk, which means both “bad luck, misfortune” and “accident”.
Borrowed from German Pedell, from Latin bidellus generalis, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *budilaz. Doublet of beul.

parole.significato: pitchblende, a black variety of uraninite
parole.testo: From pek + blende, calque of German Pechblende.

parole.significato: penis envy, the alleged desire by a woman to possess male genitalia
parole.testo: From penis + nijd (“penis”), calque of German Penisneid.
Borrowed from German Periost.
Borrowed from German Peristaltik.

parole.significato: a boarding platform on which passengers wait for a train: it is next to a spoor
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Perron, from French perron, from Middle French perron, from Old French [Term?].
Borrowed from German Pessimismus or French pessimisme.
Borrowed from German piekfein, from Low German püükfein, piekfein, wherein the former element is itself borrowed from Dutch puik.
From pikken + orde, calque of German Hackordnung.
Borrowed from German Pils, short for Pilsener (Bier).

Probably borrowed from German Pistole, from Middle French pistole, from Middle High German pitschal, pischulle, from Czech píšťala (“whistle”), from Proto-Slavic *piščalь, from *piskati, *piščati (“to squeak, whistle”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pīṣk-.
Borrowed from German Pietismus.
From plank (“plank”) + -en- + koorts (“fever”), calque of German Plankenfieber.
Borrowed from German plastisch.

parole.significato: plebeian (of the plebs, of the common people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German plebejisch, from French plébéien, from Latin plebeius.

parole.significato: a seasoned and smoked sausage made from pork and beef, similar to cervelat and salami
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Plockwurst, which see for more.
From earlier plotzelijk, plotselijk, from Early New High German plötzlich.
Probably from German pochen.
Borrowed from German Pudel. Cognate with English poodle.

parole.significato: book that is passed around between friends to write poems in
parole.testo: Orthographic borrowing from German Poesiealbum. The pronunciation was altered by association with poesie (colloquial or childish diminutive of poes).
Borrowed from German putzen. Attested since 1645.
Borrowed from German polemisch.
Borrowed from German Poliklinik.
Borrowed from German Politiker, from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós). Equivalent to politiek + -er.
From politie + staat, calque of German Polizeistaat.
Borrowed from German Politur, from Latin polītūra.
Early modern borrowing from German Poltergeist.

parole.significato: a felt or leather tip of a cue
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pomerancien, from German Pomeranze, from Medieval Latin pomerancium, from pomum (“fruit”) + arancia (“orange”).

parole.significato: punch (tool for punching or drilling holes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Punze.
Calque of German possierlich. While the spelling of potsierlijk likely was influenced by sierlijk, the two words are otherwise etymologically unrelated.
Calque of German Poesiealbum. By surface analysis, poëzie + album.

parole.significato: of, from or related to the Czech capital Prague

First attested in the late 18th century. Compound of pralen (“to show off”) + Hans, likely a calque of German Prahlhans.
From pracht + -ig, perhaps a calque of German prächtig.

Borrowed from German Praktikum, a coinage from the neuter of Late Latin practicus (“practical”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).
Borrowed from German praktisch. The adverb meaning “almost always” is a semantic loan from English practically.
From pressen + kop, a calque of German Presskopf.
Borrowed from German privatisieren. The sense “to privatise” is likely a semantic loan.
Borrowed from German problematisch. Equivalent to probleem + -atisch.
Borrowed from German prozentuell. Equivalent to procent + -eel.
From proeven (“to test”) + stand, calque of German Prüfstand.
probably borrowed from German Profi.

parole.significato: a badly mannered person; someone who uses a lot of vulgar language; a vulgarian
parole.testo: 1897, borrowed from German Prolet, from German Proletarier. Ultimately from Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”).
Borrowed from German Proletariat, from French prolétariat. Equivalent to proletariër + -aat.
From German proletarisch.

Around 1848. Borrowed from German Proletarier. Ultimately from Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”)
Either from propagandist + -isch or borrowed from German propagandistisch.
Borrowed from German prosodisch. Equivalent to prosodie + -isch.

parole.significato: food supplies, edible provision, in particular when travelling
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Proviant, in turn borrowed from Italian provianda.
Borrowed from German provisorisch.
Borrowed from German prosaisch, from French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus. By surface analysis, proza + -isch.
Probably borrowed from German psychiatrisch. Equivalent to psychiater + -isch.
Borrowed from German psychologisch.
Borrowed from German Psychose. First attested in the mid nineteenth century.
Borrowed from German psychotisch or natively formed from psychose + -isch.
Borrowed from German Putsch.
Borrowed from German Putschist. Equivalent to putsch + -ist.

parole.significato: short and stocky in figure, mesomorphic
parole.testo: From German, which itself is from Ancient Greek πυκνός (puknós, “thick”). Cognate with English pyknic.
Borrowed from German Quatsch.
Borrowed from German Rabatt.
Borrowed from German radieren.
From German Rakel.

Borrowed from German Ränzel.

Borrowed from German ranzeln, from or related to Middle High German rantzen (“to jump wildly, move around”), which is possibly related to Old High German hranca (“tendril”), in which case a doublet of rank.

parole.significato: a mother who neglects her children; a bad mother
parole.testo: From raaf (“raven”) + -en- + moeder (“mother”). Calque of German Rabenmutter.
From German reagieren. By surface analysis, re- + ageren.

Borrowed from German rechtens.
From recht + -matig, calque of German rechtmäßig.

parole.significato: nation of laws, constitutional state, (state which has rule of law)
parole.testo: Around the 1860s. From recht + -s- + staat, calque of German Rechtsstaat.
Borrowed from German Redner during the sixteenth century.
Borrowed from German Referat, from Latin referat.

parole.significato: reflexive (mostly in grammar terms like reflexive verb)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German reflexiv. Equivalent to reflexie + -ief.
From reformatie + -orisch or borrowed from German reformatorisch.

From regen + woud, a calque of German Regenwald.
Compound of reiken + wijdte, calque of German Reichweite.
From reis (“travel, voyage”) + bureau (“office, agency”). Attested since the 1890s. Probably after German Reisebüro (older Reis(e)bureau, since 1868). Compare Danish rejsebureau, Norwegian reisebyrå.

parole.significato: a state of peace and (some measure of) toleration among different religions or denominations
parole.testo: From older religionsvrede, partial calque of German Religionsfriede Equivalent to religie (“religion”) + vrede (“peace”).
From rennen + dier, calque of German Rentier, by folk etymology from older Reentier.
Borrowed from German richtig. Equivalent to recht + -ig.

parole.significato: chivalric, knightly (pertaining to or in accordance with chivalry; bestowing knighthood)
parole.testo: From ridder + -matig, calque of German rittermäßig.
From rijk + -s- + daalder, calque of German Reichstaler.

Borrowed from German rhythmisch. Equivalent to ritme + -isch.
Borrowed from German Robinsonade.

parole.significato: group of animals, especially a pack of wolves
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Rudel. First attested in the nineteenth century.

parole.significato: a serving of scrambled eggs; (uncountable) scrambled eggs
parole.testo: From roeren (“to stir, scramble”) + ei (“egg”), probably a calque of German Rührei.
Borrowed from German Rutschbahn. By surface analysis, roetsjen + baan.
Borrowed from German rutschen. Cf. Middle Dutch rutsen, a form that is obsolete in Dutch.
From roffelen + vuur, calque of German Trommelfeuer.

parole.significato: rollmop, rollmops (rolled herring, often with a filling of pickles and onions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Rollmops.
Mid-1920s, from rollen + trap, a calque of German Rolltreppe and/or French escalier roulant (both ca. 1900).
Borrowed from German Romantik.

parole.significato: excessive exploitation, of cultivated land or other resources; predatory cultivation
parole.testo: From roven (“to rob, take away”) + bouw (“exploitation”), calque of German Raubbau.

parole.significato: a predatory species, which kills and eats prey
parole.testo: From roven (“to rob, to capture”) + dier (“animal”), perhaps a calque of German Raubtier. Compare roven.
Borrowed from German Rubidium.
Fixed compound of rug + -e- + spraak, calque of German Rücksprache or Low German [Term?], ultimately from Middle Low German ruggesprake. First attested in the seventeenth century.

From rug (“back”) + zak (“sack”), calque of German Rucksack, originating from Swiss German. The figurative sense refers to the notion of trauma or issues as things one carries with oneself during life.

parole.significato: space shuttle, space vessel capable of travelling repeatedly between Earth and outer space
parole.testo: From ruimte (“space”) + veer (“ferry”). Apparently not attested before 1982, hence after German Raumfähre (early 1960s). Mainly translates English space shuttle.
Borrowed from German Rune, from Old Norse rún.
Borrowed from German Römertopf.
Borrowed from German Röntgen. Named after the German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen.
Unadapted borrowing from German rücksichtslos.
From samen (“together”) + horen (“to belong”) + -heid, calque of German Zusammengehörigkeit. Cognate with Swedish samhörighet.

parole.significato: sabre (Commonwealth), saber (US) (sword with a narrow, slightly curved blade)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Sabel, obsolete form of Säbel, from Polish szabla, from Hungarian szablya.
Borrowed from German Saffian, ultimately from Persian [Term?].
Borrowed from German Sachse. The inherited cognate is the dated and now rare Sas.
Borrowed from German salonfähig.

parole.significato: an explosive or highly flammable compound used in various explosives such as early artillery projectiles
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Satz.
Borrowed from German satirisch. Equivalent to satire + -isch.
Borrowed from German Saurier or English saurian. First attested in the 1830s.

parole.significato: to scalp, to remove haired skin from
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from German skalpieren, from English scalp. Equivalent to scalp + -eren.
From German skeptisch, a learned borrowing of Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós, “thoughtful, inquiring”).

Borrowed from German Skala and/or English scale, from Latin scāla. The earlier borrowing Middle Dutch scale (“ladder”) had become very rare or was even lost entirely in early modern Dutch, implying that it was later reintroduced in the contemporary sense.
From schamen (“to (be a)shame(d)”) + haar (“hair”), calque of German Schamhaar, though note that the first element in the German word is a noun. The oldest citations in Dutch use the plural form.

parole.significato: a pair of scissor binoculars; a pair of adjustable stereoscopic binoculars consisting of two (short) periscopes
parole.testo: From schaar (“pair of scissors”) + verrekijker (“pair of binoculars, telescope”), calque of German Scherenfernrohr. First attested in 1915.
Borrowed from German Schadenfreude.
From schade + vreugde, a calque of German Schadenfreude (“schadenfreude”).
Borrowed from German schaffen. Doublet of scheppen.

parole.significato: a sconce or a similar type of fortification
parole.testo: From German Schanze; cognate with English sconce.
Borrowed from German Schelm or Middle Low German schelm.

parole.significato: trickster novel, picaresque novel ((proto)novel about tricksters)
parole.testo: 19th century. From schelm (“trickster, scoundrel”) + -en- + roman (“novel”), calque of German Schelmenroman.
From scherp + -zinnig, calque of German scharfsinnig.
From schijn (“shine”) + werper (“thrower”), calque of German Scheinwerfer.
From schild + klier, calque of German Schilddrüse.

Borrowed from German Schminke.
Borrowed from German schminken. By surface analysis, schmink + -en.

parole.significato: to do work as a gig or a side job
parole.testo: Borrowed from German schnabeln.
Borrowed from German Schnitzel.

parole.significato: a pedant, notably a teacher who loves finding and correcting faults; an unpleasant teacher
parole.testo: From school + vos, calque of German Schulfuchs.

parole.significato: pedantry, in particular when done by teachers
parole.testo: From schoolvos + -erij, perhaps a calque of German Schulfuchserei.

parole.significato: a lapdog, a canine pet which is small and/or frequently cuddled
parole.testo: From schoot (“lap”) + hond (“hond”), perhaps a calque of German Schoßhund.
Via Early Modern German schüchter from a German Low German [Term?] source. The contemporary German form is schüchtern. Eventually akin to German scheu, Dutch schuw, and English shy.

parole.significato: to brush (usually with a flat brush)
parole.testo: First attested in the 16th century. Borrowed from German scheuern, itself probably from Middle Dutch schuren. In any case a doublet of schuren, which see.

parole.significato: debt brake, balanced budget (measures enacted to prevent the growth of national debt)
parole.testo: Compound of schuld (“debt”) + -en- + rem (“brake”), calque of German Schuldenbremse.
Borrowed from German Schurke. Attested since at least 1701.

parole.significato: dive, a deliberate fall to gain advantage in the game
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Schwalbe (“swallow, deliberate fall”), a cognate and thus a doublet of zwaluw. From a saying „Der fliegt wie ’ne Schwalbe!“ (“The man flies like a swallow!”), or the like, punning on German fliegen in its colloquial sense “to fall”.

parole.significato: a bastard, an arse; used as a stereotypically German insult.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Schweinehund.
From German schwul.
From German Schwung, from the German verb schwingen.

parole.significato: secretion, that which has been secreted
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Sekret or from secretie.
A borrowing from German Selen or Swedish selen, or a shortening of selenium, as seleen is attested considerably later than selenium.

From Middle Dutch tzitteren (15th c.), from Early Modern German zittern, from Proto-Germanic *titrōną, whence also English teeter and (perhaps) dither.
Borrowed in early modern times from German Zierat (“ornament, decoration”) (modern spelling Zierrat).

Borrowed from German Sitz im Leben.

Borrowed from German Schabracke, Hungarian csáprág and Turkish čaprak.

parole.significato: to sell a pup, to swindle with substandard wares, to scam
parole.testo: Borrowed from German schachern (“to haggle”), from Yiddish סחרן (sakhern, “to trade”), from Hebrew סַחַר (sakhár, “commerce”).
Borrowed from German Schärpe.
From German schummeln (“to cheat, to swindle”).

parole.significato: skeleton (support structure of an organism; ensemble of animal bones)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Skelett, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”), from σκελλώ (skellṓ, “to dry, dry up, to make dry, to parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”).
Borrowed from German Schlagrahm. By surface analysis, slag (“to strike”) + room (“cream”).

parole.significato: a simple sentimental popular song about a sad story, usually involving love, death, nostalgia or illness, of a genre or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Schmachtlappen, but by folk etymology reanalysed as smart (“grief”) + lap (“rag, sheet”). From smeren + kaas, calque of German Schmierkäse.
Borrowed from German Schnapphahn (“robber on horseback”). Equivalent to snappen (“to get, to apprehend”) + haan (“rooster, cock”).

parole.significato: a period or instance of heavy snowfall
parole.testo: From sneeuw + bom, calque of German Schneebombe.

parole.significato: a shandy; a cocktail made with beer and lemonade (often 7 Up)
parole.testo: From sneeuw (“snow”) + wit (“white”) + -je (diminutive suffix), calque of German Schneewittchen.

From sociaal (“social”) + democraat (“democrat”), calque of German Sozialdemokrat.
From sociaal + democratie, calque of German Sozialdemokratie.

Unadapted borrowing from German sowieso. The negated sense niet sowieso (“not necessarily”), used in the Netherlands, does not exist in German, which uses nicht unbedingt instead. Belgian Dutch uses the equivalent expression niet per se, which is also used in the Netherlands.
From sparen (“to save (up)”) + geld (“money”), calque of German Spargeld.
Borrowed from German Spat.

parole.significato: splits (move in dance or gymnastics in which the legs are extended straight out and perpendicular to the body)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Spagat, from Italian spaccata.

parole.significato: specialised study, investigation of a specific subject
parole.testo: From speciaal (“special”) + studie (“study”), calque of German Spezialstudium.
Probably borrowed from German Sperrdifferential. Equivalent to sperren + differentieel.

parole.significato: to cheat, to crib (at a test or game)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German spicken.

parole.significato: mere play; a game; nothing serious
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Spielerei.
From spierkracht (“muscle power”) + vliegtuig (“aeroplane, airplane”), calque of German Muskelkraftflugzeug.

parole.significato: a rod used for spinning and winding natural fibres; a spindle

Borrowed from German Sprit.

parole.significato: piped or pressed swirly butter cookies formed with a pastry bag

parole.significato: top to bottom of a balance sheet or budget page
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Staffel (“stairs”).
Compound of staf + rijm, a nineteenth-century Romantic calque of German Stabreim.

parole.significato: a Katyusha (Soviet artillery multiple rocket launcher)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Stalinorgel. Equivalent to Stalin + orgel.
Compound of stam + cel, calque of German Stammzelle.

parole.significato: stem duchy (one of the duchies of the Carolingian Empire that originated from tribal kingdoms, traditionally counted as…

parole.significato: sedentary wild animals (wild animals of a non-migratory population)

parole.significato: in a student-like, often also jocular, way

parole.significato: antiking, especially in an electoral monarchy

parole.significato: a symbolic action (action that conveys a message or symbolism)

From zelf + genoeg + -zaam, perhaps a calque of German selbstgenügsam.
From zelf- (“self-”) + moord (“murder”). A calque of German Selbstmord, from New Latin suīcīdium.
From zelf- + stand + -ig, calque of German selbstständig. First attested in the late sixteenth century. Compare also English selfstanding.
Borrowed from German Selbstvertrauen. Equivalent to zelf + vertrouwen.
From zelf- (“self-”) + zeker (“certain”), calque of German selbstsicher (“confident”).
Borrowed from German Zeppelin, from the surname of Ferdinand Adolf Heinrich August Graf von Zeppelin, named after Zepelin in Mecklenburg.

parole.significato: zugzwang (situation in which a disadvantageous move is forced)
parole.testo: From zet + dwang, calque of German Zugzwang.
Borrowed from German Sichel. Doublet of sikkel (“sickle”).

parole.significato: to know with whom one is dealing, (especially) to know one's people
parole.testo: Calque of German seine Pappenheimer kennen.
Calque of German seinerseits. By surface analysis, zijner + zijde + -s.

parole.significato: one of certain herons of the genera Ardea and Egretta that have white plumage; roughly corresponding to egret but used…
parole.testo: From zilver (“silver”) + reiger (“heron”), calque of German Silberreiher. First attested in the early to mid nineteenth century.
Borrowed from German Zink.
From zin + -e- + beeld, calque of German Sinnbild.
From zin + -vol, calque of German sinnvoll.

Onomatopoeic, perhaps borrowed from German summen.

parole.significato: mammal, any member of the class Mammalia
parole.testo: From zogen + dier, calque of German Säugetier. First attested in the 1800s.
Borrowed from German zoroastrisch, equivalent to Zoroaster + -isch. First attested in the mid 19th century.

Borrowed from German Zoroastrier, equivalent to Zoroaster + -iër. First attested in the late 19th century.

parole.significato: zugzwang (situation in which a disadvantageous move is forced on a player)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zugzwang.

parole.significato: suckling, infant which isn't weaned yet
parole.testo: 16th century. From zuigen + -e- + -ling, calque of German Säugling.
From zuigen + nap, likely a calque of German Saugnapf.
Borrowed from German zum Kotzen, the latter being the gerund of kotzen (compare kotsen and om te kotsen).

parole.significato: bandwagon effect, or a group resulting from it
parole.testo: After German Schwan, kleb an ("Swan, stick to"), a fairy tale written by Ludwig Bechstein. In the story, a boy finds a swan which makes people stick to it when they are touching it, if the boy says the titular phrase. By surface analysis, zwaan + kleef aan, imperative of aankleven.
Calque of German schwachsinnig. Equivalent to zwak + zin + -ig, literally, “weak of senses”.
Borrowed from German Schwanz.
From zwindelen, from Middle Dutch swindelen. Equivalent to zwinden (“to disappear”) + -elen. The sense “to swindle” is a semantic loan from German schwindeln and possibly English swindle.
From zwerven + woord, calque of German Wanderwort.

parole.significato: at all; anyway; in the first place
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German überhaupt.
